questions.prompt: A learned model explains 99% of the variance of next states in logged data. What can you conclude about its usefulness for planning?
options: It will beat any other model that has a lower explained variance in the logs.
Nothing yet: planning depends on how it ranks actions, which only planning tests.
It must have learned the effect of the actions correctly, since the fit is good.
It is safe to plan with it over any horizon, because the fit is so high.
questions.explanation: High explained variance can come from the action-independent part of the dynamics; usefulness is a decision-level property.

questions.prompt: True x'=0.9x, learned x'=0.95x, zero actions, x0=2. What is the open-loop prediction error (learned minus true) after 10 steps? (3 decimals)
CEM planning uses N=200 samples, horizon H=10 and 3 iterations. How many model evaluations (single-step predictions) per replan?
Why does model predictive control (replanning every step) tolerate model errors better than executing a long open-loop plan?
options: It uses a more accurate model, so every prediction contains much less error to begin with.
It does not need a model at all, since it only reacts to the latest observation.
It plans over much longer horizons, so the prediction errors average out over time.
Each plan starts from the real observed state, so errors cannot build up past the horizon.
questions.explanation: Feedback resets the state estimate every step.

questions.prompt: A one-step model has MSE 0.02 on next states whose variance is 0.5. What is its explained variance? (2 decimals)
A model ignores the action input entirely. When a random-shooting planner evaluates 100 candidate action sequences with it, what happens?
options: The planner picks the best candidate by the chance of small noise in the model.
The planner picks the candidate with the smallest actions, since they cost least.
All candidates get the same predicted outcome, so selection is arbitrary.
The planner selects the longest sequence, since it has the most steps to evaluate.
questions.explanation: Identical predictions mean no ranking information.

questions.prompt: Design an experiment to decide between two world models, one with lower pixel/state prediction error and one with higher. State the metric, the baseline, a held-out condition and what would reject your preferred model.
rubric: Uses a decision-level metric (real task success or cost after planning), not just prediction error.
Includes a baseline (random or no-model) and several seeds or start states.
States in advance a result that would reject the preference, e.g. the lower-error model failing to beat the baseline.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
